theory_name: Coupled thermoelasticity formulated through irreversible thermodynamics, in terms of an entropy displacement vector
heat_law_equation_ref: eq (3.3) and eq (3.4), printed p.242; entropy-flux form eq (6.11)2, printed p.245
heat_law_in_words: (3.3): dh/dt = k div grad theta = k laplacian theta, with k the coefficient of heat conduction. With h = c theta + T beta e this gives (3.4): k laplacian theta = c dtheta/dt + T beta de/dt. In the variational treatment the same law appears as (6.11)2: grad theta + (rho T / k) dS/dt = 0, where S is the entropy displacement vector.
relaxation_parameters: not found in the heat conduction law: no relaxation time and no relaxation symbol enters (3.3), (3.4) or (6.11)2. The word relaxation occurs only in the operational solution of the conduction problem: 'relaxation modes' (printed p.247) and a 'continuous relaxation spectrum ... for the relaxation constants lambda' (printed p.251).
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: printed p.250: 'The dilatational wave propagates with a diffuse front, characterized by a finite group velocity and an infinite signal velocity.' The next sentences add that 'Rotational waves are unaffected by the thermal phenomenon and propagate with no attenuation or dispersion at the velocity (mu/rho)^(1/2).' No dispersion relation is derived.
conditions_stated_by_source: 'The second law of thermodynamics requires that ds be an exact differential' in the temperature and the strain components (printed p.241, leading to (2.7); the printed symbols are partly obscured in the scan). The thermoelastic potential V and the dissipation function D 'are then positive definite quadratic forms' (printed p.246, eq (8.2)). No explicit sign condition on k and no bound on any relaxation time is stated in printed pp.240-253.
dissipation_statement: The Abstract, printed p.240, presents the theory through a 'dissipation function in terms of the time derivative of an entropy displacement'. Printed p.246 introduces an invariant D 'which plays the role of a dissipation function', notes that it 'may be shown to measure the rate of entropy production', and gives the rate of entropy production due to a temperature gradient in (7.15)-(7.16). Printed p.250 defines the generalized dissipation function D in (11.4).

source_doi: not found printed on the page (the file name carries the ASME article number 1.2822329, but no DOI is printed in the article)
theory_name: Dual-phase-lag heat conduction, presented as a unified field approach from macro- to micro-scales
heat_law_equation_ref: eq (1), printed p.8; expanded form eq (2), printed p.9; energy equation (3) and heat equations (4), (5), printed p.9
heat_law_in_words: (1): q(r,t + tauq) = -K grad T(r,t + tauT), a constitutive equation with a lag in the heat flux and a lag in the temperature gradient. A first-order expansion gives (2): q + tauq dq/dt = -K[grad T + tauT d/dt(grad T)]. Combined with the energy equation (3), -div q = Cp dT/dt, elimination of q gives (4): laplacian T + tauT d/dt(laplacian T) = (1/alpha) dT/dt + (tauq/alpha) d2T/dt2; elimination of T gives the flux form (5).
relaxation_parameters: tauq, the phase lag of the heat flux (the relaxation time), and tauT, the phase lag of the temperature gradient. Printed p.8: 'The phase lags tauq and tauT are both positive'. The coefficient tauq/alpha is identified with 1/C^2, C being the thermal wave speed (printed p.9).
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: printed p.9: 'The coefficient tauq/alpha in front of the wave terms in both equations is defined as 1/C^2, with C being the thermal wave speed (Chester, 1963).' No dispersion relation is derived. Printed p.12 reports that a sharp wave front exists for tauT = 0, that any small tauT destroys it, and that tauq = tauT reduces (4) to the diffusion equation.
conditions_stated_by_source: 'The phase lags tauq and tauT are both positive and assumed to be intrinsic properties' (printed p.8, the last words partly cut in the scan); printed p.12: 'A more general condition for the reduction of the universal model to diffusion ... is tauq = tauT (not necessarily equal to zero)'.
dissipation_statement: printed p.12: 'the diffusion term ... provides damping to the heat flow', and the mixed-derivative term 'provides a negative damping, a counterbalanced effect to diffusion, to heat propagation'. Printed p.16: 'the wave behavior vanishes due to the negative sign in front of the wave term'. The model is never described as dissipation-free.
notes: Read from the text layer and page images of B13-025__1.2822329.pdf (9 PDF pages = printed 8-16; printed page = PDF page + 7). Running heads read '8 / Vol. 117, FEBRUARY 1995, Transactions of the ASME' and 'Journal of Heat Transfer'. Equation (4) was checked on the page image because the text layer garbles the symbols.

source_doi: 10.1080/01495730601130919 (printed on the cover sheet and on printed p.232)
theory_name: Three-phase-lag thermoelasticity, with phase lags in the heat flux, the temperature gradient and the thermal displacement gradient
heat_law_equation_ref: eq (3), printed p.233; first-order form eq (4), printed p.233; Green-Naghdi type III law eq (2), printed p.233
heat_law_in_words: (3): q(P, t + tauq) = -[k grad T(P, t + tauT) + k* grad v(P, t + tauv)]. First-order expansion (4): q + tauq dq/dt = -[tau*v grad T + k tauT d/dt grad T + k* grad v], with tau*v = k + k* tauv, written after the intermediate form k(grad T + tauT d/dt grad T) + k*(grad v + tauv grad T). Eq (2) is the Green-Naghdi law q = -(k grad T + k* grad v).
relaxation_parameters: tauq, tauT and tauv, the phase lags of the heat flux, of the temperature gradient and of the thermal displacement gradient (printed p.233). The paper states that 'the phase lags tauq and tauT are small, positive' and assumes '0 <= tauv < tauT < tauq'; k* > 0 is a material constant of the theory (printed p.233).
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: not found as an explicit formula: no wave speed and no dispersion relation is printed. The paper states instead that the field equations (9) and (10) 'admit damped thermoelastic solutions' (printed p.234), that the two-phase-lag reduction admits 'damped thermoelastic wave solutions' (printed p.235), and that the Green-Naghdi type II limit admits undamped waves (printed p.236).
conditions_stated_by_source: '0 <= tauv < tauT < tauq' (printed p.233, the assumption on the three delay times); 'the phase lags tauq and tauT are small, positive' (printed p.233); k* > 0 (printed p.233). No further stability inequality is stated in printed pp.231-238.
dissipation_statement: printed p.234: the three-phase-lag system 'admits damped thermo-elastic solutions due to the presence of the temperature-rate term'. Printed p.235: the two-phase-lag reduction 'admits damped thermoelastic wave solutions'. Printed p.236, discussion items 4 and 5: the Green-Naghdi type II limit is 'without energy dissipation' and admits undamped waves, while type III admits damped thermoelastic waves.
notes: Read from the text layer of B07-021__On A Thermoelastic Three-Phase-Lag Mode.pdf (9 PDF pages: a Taylor and Francis cover sheet plus printed 231-238; printed page = PDF page + 229). theory_name: Moore-Gibson-Thompson thermoelasticity, obtained by adding a relaxation parameter to the Green-Naghdi type III heat conduction
heat_law_equation_ref: eq (1.2), printed p.1 (Maxwell-Cattaneo, quoted); eq (2.4), printed p.3 (MGT); eq (2.5), printed p.3
heat_law_in_words: (1.2): tau dq_i/dt + q_i = k u_,i, quoted as the Maxwell-Cattaneo law. (2.4): tau dq_i/dt + q_i = (k_ij u_,j) + (k*_ij alpha_,j), with tau > 0, alpha being the thermal displacement (alpha-dot = u); together with q_i,i = c u-dot (2.2) it gives the MGT equation (2.5). For k* = 0 the law returns to Maxwell-Cattaneo, for tau = 0 it is the Green-Naghdi type III law q_i = k* alpha_,i + k u_,i.
relaxation_parameters: tau, called the relaxation parameter, 'which is assumed to be positive' (printed p.1, after eq (1.2)); tau > 0 is stated again in (2.4) on printed p.3. No other relaxation parameter appears in the paper.
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: not found as a formula: no wave speed and no dispersion relation is printed. Only qualitative statements: with the Maxwell-Cattaneo law 'a damped hyperbolic equation is obtained ... the thermal waves propagate with finite speed' (printed p.1), while the type III law 'allows the propagation of thermal waves with infinite speed and violates the causality principle' (printed pp.2-3).
conditions_stated_by_source: tau > 0 (printed pp.1 and 3); (i) c(x) >= c0 > 0, (ii) k*_ij xi_i xi_j >= k0 xi_i xi_i, (iii) K_ij xi_i xi_j >= k1 xi_i xi_i with K_ij = k_ij - tau k*_ij, eqs (2.8)-(2.9), printed p.3; and (2.10) k_ij xi_i xi_j >= k2 xi_i xi_i, stated to follow from the second law.
dissipation_statement: printed p.2: the Green-Naghdi type II theory has 'no dissipation'. Printed p.4: the energy identity E(t) + F(t) = E(0) with F(t) the integral of K_ij u-dot_,i u-dot_,j, eqs (2.11)-(2.13), and 'the exponential decay of the solutions can be proved'. Printed p.9, Theorem 4.7: the semigroup is exponentially stable. Printed p.10: instability when k < k* tau.
